common_name: Chomley Farran Carnation (Historic Striped Bizarre-Type Border Carnation)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Chomley Farran is a slow-growing heirloom border carnation best increased by cuttings or layering rather than seed.

directions: Chomley Farran is one of the last surviving representatives of the striped Bizarre carnations bred and prized by 18th- and 19th-century florists' societies, most of which have since vanished from cultivation; its large, fully double, fragrant flowers are smoky lavender-grey heavily flaked and striped with vivid fuchsia-red over glaucous, blue-grey evergreen foliage. Grow it as a border carnation with sharp drainage and full sun, and stake taller stems if needed since the fully double flowers can be heavy. Take cuttings or divide congested clumps periodically to maintain vigor, since old carnation clumps decline if left too long undivided.

common_name: Musgrave's Pink Dianthus (Fragrant White Cottage Pink with Green Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this heirloom cottage pink forms a loose, grassy grey-green mat that is easily lifted and divided.

directions: Musgrave's Pink is a historic cottage pink reputedly grown in English gardens since the 1700s and a longtime holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit. Its single, fringed, pure white flowers are set off by a distinctive pale green eye and carry a strong, sweet clove fragrance over a loose mat of narrow, grey-green, grass-like evergreen foliage. Shear lightly after the main flush to tidy the mat, and divide every few years in fall to keep clumps vigorous and free-flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Becky Robinson forms a compact mound of glaucous foliage and divides readily.

directions: Becky Robinson is a modern classic laced pink, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, bearing fragrant, semi-double, pale rose-pink flowers with a deep maroon-red eye and lacing that traces each petal edge in the historic laced-pink pattern. Its compact mound of narrow, blue-grey evergreen foliage stays neat through the season, and stems rarely need staking. Deadhead to prolong bloom and divide every few years in fall to keep clumps floriferous.

common_name: Bovey Belle Dianthus (Double Purple Allwoodii Border Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Bovey Belle is a vigorous Allwoodii Group hybrid pink that benefits from being lifted and divided every few years.

directions: Bovey Belle is a strong-growing Allwoodii Group pink, a hybrid group derived from crosses between Dianthus caryophyllus and D. plumarius, holding the RHS Award of Garden Merit, bearing lightly scented, fully double, bright purple to deep magenta flowers on stems taller and more upright than mat-forming cheddar pinks, making it a useful mid-border filler and excellent cut flower. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage, deadhead to extend bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Telstar Picotee Dianthus (AAS-Winning Interspecific Picotee Pink)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or plant nursery starts a few weeks before to shortly after the last frost into full sun; Telstar is an interspecific hybrid between Sweet William and China Pink bred for hardiness and heavy branching.

directions: Plant nursery-grown starts or direct seedlings into well-drained soil in full sun. Telstar Picotee is part of the AAS-winning Telstar series, an interspecific dianthus hybrid combining the hardiness and floriferousness of Sweet William with the compact habit and season-long bloom of China Pink; its ruffled, spicy-fragrant flowers are picotee-edged, with a lighter center bordered in a darker contrasting hue. The series is valued for heat tolerance, heavy branching, and good disease resistance compared to older bedding dianthus strains, blooming from spring into fall without requiring deadheading. Keep soil well-drained, since dianthus is prone to crown rot in wet conditions.

common_name: Buena Vista English Lavender (Twice-Blooming Deep Blue Lavender)

planting.note: Transplant rooted cuttings after the last frost into lean, well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun; Buena Vista is a rebloomer that benefits from deadheading by midsummer to encourage a second flush.

directions: Bred in Oregon, Buena Vista is a hard-to-find twice-blooming English lavender, producing its first flush of elongated, bi-colored spikes, dark blue-violet calyxes with lighter blue corollas, in late spring, then reblooming in late summer into fall. Deadhead spent spikes by midsummer to encourage the second flush, and shear the whole plant back by about a third after the final bloom to keep growth compact and woody. Give it excellent drainage and avoid summer irrigation once established, since wet feet are the most common cause of failure.

common_name: Sweet Romance Lavender (Proven Winners First-Year-Flowering English Lavender)

planting.note: Transplant nursery starts after the last frost into lean, well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun; Sweet Romance was bred to flower reliably in its first year with little or no vernalization.

directions: Sweet Romance is a Proven Winners English lavender selection forming dense, compact mounds of silvery-grey foliage topped with rich violet-purple flower spikes from early summer into early fall, and it is notable for its ability to bloom the first year from a young plant with little or no cold vernalization required. It is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving in hot, dry, gravelly sites where many perennials struggle. Shear the foliage back hard in early spring to rejuvenate growth, but avoid heavy fall pruning since the woody structure protects the crown through winter.

common_name: Platinum Blonde Lavandin (Variegated Cream-Edged Foliage Lavender)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; Platinum Blonde is a sterile lavandin sport that must be propagated vegetatively and grows larger than English lavenders.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry, neutral-to-alkaline soil, sheltered from harsh winter wind. Platinum Blonde was discovered as a sport by a Spanish breeder and was nominated for Plant of the Year at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show; it is grown chiefly for its striking variegated foliage, narrow, grey-green leaves edged in creamy yellow, which provides season-long color even between bloom cycles, topped in summer by fragrant spikes of soft blue flowers. Like other lavandins it grows larger and more vigorously than English lavender, so allow extra space for airflow, and shear lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, compact mound.

common_name: Ellagance Purple English Lavender (Seed-Grown Dark Purple-Blue Lavender)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Ellagance Purple is a seed-grown English lavender bred for uniformity, earliness, and strong first-year flowering.

directions: Sow seed indoors under lights, barely covering it since light aids germination, and transplant into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil after frost danger has passed. Ellagance Purple produces long, strong stems topped with large, dense, fragrant flower spikes, dark purple buds opening to rich purple-blue blooms, over compact, spreading mounds of grey-green foliage, and it was bred for excellent uniformity, earliness, and spike quality compared to older seed strains. It is winter-hardy and blooms reliably the first year from an early sowing, making it useful for both bedding displays and permanent perennial plantings. Keep water low once established, since drainage matters more than fertility to long-term survival.

common_name: Ellagance Snow English Lavender (Seed-Grown White Lavender)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Ellagance Snow does not require cold stratification but needs plenty of light and warmth to germinate evenly.

directions: Sow seed indoors under lights, barely covering it since light aids germination; Ellagance Snow germinates without cold stratification but needs consistent warmth and bright light. Transplant into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil after frost danger has passed. It bears pure white flower spikes on strong, long stems above silvery-green foliage, standing out as an accent among purple-flowered lavenders in mixed plantings or as a monochrome display on its own. Like other Ellagance series lavenders it is compact, uniform, and winter-hardy, blooming reliably in its first year from an early sowing. Keep water low once established and avoid rich, moisture-retentive soils that shorten its lifespan.

common_name: Giles van Hees Speedwell (Dwarf Rose-Pink Spike Speedwell)

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; this dwarf spike speedwell forms a tidy, compact clump well suited to the front of the border.

directions: Giles van Hees is a compact, clump-forming spike speedwell producing upright spikes of star-shaped, rose-pink flowers that open from the base upward from early to late summer, held above a bushy mound of lance-shaped, bright green leaves. Its small stature makes it an excellent choice for the front of a sunny border, edging, or containers, where it delivers a long-lasting impact without sprawling. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, deadhead spent spikes to prolong the bloom season, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Blauriesin Speedwell (Blue Giant Tall Garden Speedwell)

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Blauriesin is one of the tallest garden speedwells and benefits from staking in exposed sites.

directions: Also sold as Blue Giant or Blue Giantess, Blauriesin is an upright, bushy garden speedwell forming dense, terminal racemes of deep lavender-blue flowers on tall stems, among the tallest of the commonly grown speedwells and an excellent choice for cutting. It thrives in consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, unlike drought-tolerant rock-garden veronicas, and benefits from staking or growing among sturdier neighbors in windy sites. Deadheading spent spikes weekly extends bloom from early summer well into early fall; divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Royal Blue Speedwell (Hungarian Speedwell with Vivid Deep Blue Flowers)

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; trim plants back by half after the first flush to keep the sprawling habit compact and to encourage rebloom.

directions: Royal Blue is a selection of saw-leaved or Hungarian speedwell, forming mounding to sprawling clumps clad in toothed, oblong green leaves and topped from late spring through summer, and often again into fall, by dense, erect racemes of star-shaped, vivid deep blue flowers. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, avoiding wet or poorly drained sites. Trim plants back by about half after the main flush to tidy the sprawling mature foliage and to prompt a late-season rebloom; propagate readily by division or cuttings.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; this silver-leaved speedwell dislikes wet, poorly drained sites and is more likely to be lost to winter wet than winter cold.

directions: Silver Carpet is a compact, clump-forming spike speedwell grown as much for its densely hairy, silvery grey-green, serrated foliage as for its flowers, producing dense, erect racemes of small, star-shaped, purple-blue blooms from early to late summer. The silvery foliage stays attractive from spring through fall, making it a strong textural and color-contrast partner for green-leaved perennials in a sunny border or rock garden. Grow in full sun in sharply well-drained soil, since it dislikes wet feet and is more likely to be lost to winter moisture than winter cold; remove spent flower spikes to prolong bloom.
